level1.text: The handle of a gym machine is attached to a return spring whose spring constant is $250\,\text{N/m}$. The exerciser pulls the handle so that the spring stretches $0.12\,\text{m}$, and holds the handle still. How large is the force of the spring on the handle?
A spring at the edge of a trampoline stretches $0.050\,\text{m}$ when a force of $450\,\text{N}$ stretches it. What is the spring constant of the spring?
An exerciser stretches a hand spring whose spring constant is $180\,\text{N/m}$ so that the spring extends $0.15\,\text{m}$. How much elastic potential energy is stored in the spring?
The graph shows the force $F_\text{v}$ stretching a spring as a function of the extension $x$ of the spring. Read two points of the line from the graph. What is the spring constant of the spring?
The spring constant of the spring of a fisherman's spring balance is $40\,\text{N/m}$. How much does the spring stretch when a force of $6.0\,\text{N}$ stretches it? Give the answer in metres.
The force stretching a spring is directly proportional to the extension of the spring, $F_\text{v} = kx$. When does this expression describe a spring well?
level1.answer: Kun jousta ei venytetä liian pitkälle, koska liian suurella venymällä voima ei enää kasva tasaisesti.

choices.text: Only if the spring is horizontal, because the weight of a vertical spring itself spoils the proportionality.
choices.feedback: The mass of the spring itself is neglected, and the proportionality holds for a vertical spring too: the weight $mg$ of the mass is exactly the force stretching the spring, from which the spring constant is measured.

choices.text: Always, because the spring constant is a constant and so the force is proportional to the extension at all extensions.
choices.feedback: The spring constant is constant only in the working range of the spring. At too large an extension the $(x, F_\text{v})$ graph bends away from the line, and the spring may no longer return to its rest length.

choices.text: Only if the spring is compressed and not stretched, because when stretched the force is always smaller.
choices.feedback: The harmonic force holds equally well for a stretched and a compressed spring: the magnitude of the force is $k|x|$ in both cases, and only the direction changes.

choices.text: When the spring is not stretched too far, because at too large an extension the force no longer grows steadily.
choices.feedback: Correct. The harmonic force is a model that holds for small extensions. When the spring is stretched too much, the material of the spring begins to stretch in a different way or stays permanently deformed, and the line of the measurement points no longer continues.

level1.text: The extension of a spring is doubled, for example from $2.0\,\text{cm}$ to $4.0\,\text{cm}$. What happens to the elastic potential energy $E_\text{p}$ of the spring?
level1.answer: Se nelinkertaistuu, koska energia on verrannollinen venymän toiseen potenssiin.

choices.text: It doubles, because the stretching force doubles and the energy is proportional to the force.
choices.feedback: The force doubles, but the stretching is also done over a distance twice as long. So the work, that is the energy, grows more than the force.

choices.text: It stays the same, because the spring constant and the rest length of the spring do not change when stretching.
choices.feedback: The spring constant stays the same, but $E_\text{p} = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ also depends on the extension $x$, so the energy changes.

choices.text: It becomes four times as large, because the energy is proportional to the second power of the extension.
choices.feedback: Correct. The base and the height of the triangle double, so the area, that is the energy, becomes four times as large: $\tfrac{1}{2}k(2x)^2 = 4\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.

choices.text: It grows by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$, because the energy is proportional to the square root of the extension.
choices.feedback: In the formula the extension is raised to the second power, not under a square root. A square root would make the growth slower, when in reality the energy grows faster than the extension.

level1.text: The graph shows the extension and the stretching force of two springs A and B. Read two points of the line of spring B (dashed line) from the graph. What is the spring constant of spring B?

level2.text: A spring is stretched $8.0\,\text{cm}$, and the force meter then reads $6.0\,\text{N}$. How much elastic potential energy is stored in the spring?
The spring of a toy gun is compressed $6.0\,\text{cm}$, which stores $0.90\,\text{J}$ of elastic potential energy in it. What is the spring constant of the spring?

A spring whose spring constant is $150\,\text{N/m}$ is stretched $3.0\,\text{cm}$. The extension is increased to $9.0\,\text{cm}$. By how much does the elastic potential energy of the spring increase?

The forces stretching two springs A and B are shown as a function of the extension in the same graph. First determine the spring constant of spring A from the graph. Spring A is stretched $0.080\,\text{m}$. How much elastic potential energy is stored in it?

Students determined the spring constant of a spring by hanging masses on it and measuring the extension of the spring. The table shows example data from the measurement; $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$.

a) Which measurement points are in the linear range, where the force stretching the spring is directly proportional to the extension?

b) Draw the $(x, F_\text{v})$ graph and fit to the points of the linear range a line through the origin. What is the spring constant of the spring?

Give the result of part b) in the answer box.

data.caption: Extension of a spring as a function of the mass (example data)

level2.text:
A student measures the spring constant of a spring. The length of the spring without a load is $12.0\,\text{cm}$. When a mass of $0.200\,\text{kg}$ is hung on the spring, the length of the spring at rest is $20.0\,\text{cm}$. The mass of the spring is neglected; $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$.

The student calculates: “The spring is stretched by the weight of the mass $0.200\,\text{kg}\cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 = 1.962\,\text{N}$ and the length of the spring is $0.200\,\text{m}$, so $k = \dfrac{F_\text{v}}{x} = \dfrac{1.962\,\text{N}}{0.200\,\text{m}} = 9.81\,\text{N/m}$.”

What is the error in the student's calculation? Calculate the correct spring constant and give it in the answer box.

Two springs are each stretched at rest by the same stretching force $12\,\text{N}$. The spring constant of spring 1 is $80\,\text{N/m}$ and that of spring 2 is $240\,\text{N/m}$. A student claims: “More energy is stored in the stiffer spring, because it is stiffer.”

a) Calculate the extension of each spring.

b) Calculate the elastic potential energy of each spring.

c) How much more elastic potential energy is there in the softer spring than in the stiffer one? Give the result of part c) in the answer box.

level3.text: A car rests on four identical springs. When passengers with a total mass of $300\,\text{kg}$ get in, the springs are compressed a further $3.0\,\text{cm}$. The elasticity of the tyres is ignored. Assume that the extra load is shared equally by the four springs. What is the spring constant of one spring? Give the answer in $\text{kN/m}$.

A jumping toy has a vertical spring whose spring constant is $200\,\text{N/m}$. The toy is pressed against a table so that the spring is compressed $3.0\,\text{cm}$, and a suction cup holds it in place.

When the suction cup lets go, the spring launches the $50\,\text{g}$ toy straight up. Assume that all of the elastic potential energy changes into the gravitational potential energy of the toy; air resistance and the mass of the spring are neglected.

How high does the toy rise from its starting point?

A trolley of mass $0.50\,\text{kg}$ is on a horizontal frictionless track between two springs.

One end of the left spring is attached to the left wall and one end of the right spring to the right wall, and at the equilibrium position both springs are at their rest length. The spring constant of the left spring is $30\,\text{N/m}$ and that of the right spring $50\,\text{N/m}$.

The trolley is moved $4.0\,\text{cm}$ to the right and released. What is the net force on the trolley immediately after it is released?

The stretching of a rubber band was investigated by hanging forces of different sizes on it and measuring the extension of the band. The table shows example data; the force $F_\text{v}$ is the force stretching the band, and the point $(0;\ 0)$ of the graph belongs to the measurement.

a) Calculate the quotient $\dfrac{F_\text{v}}{x}$ for every measurement point other than the origin and use it to justify whether the rubber band can be described by the harmonic force $F_\text{v} = kx$ and a single spring constant.

b) Estimate the work done by the force stretching the band over the extension $12\,\text{cm}$ by calculating the area between the $(x, F_\text{v})$ graph and the $x$ axis. Divide the area into trapezoids between the measurement points: the area of a trapezoid is the width of the interval times the mean of the forces at the ends of the interval.

c) Compare the result with the energy you would get from the formula $E_\text{p} = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ when $k$ is calculated from the first measurement point.

Give the result of part b) in the answer box.

data.caption: Stretching of a rubber band (example data)

level3.text:
The pull force of the string of a crossbow was measured with a force meter when the string was pulled from its rest position to different distances. The table shows example data. The spring of the crossbow is assumed to follow the harmonic force $F_\text{v} = kx$ over the whole measured range.

After that an arrow of mass $25\,\text{g}$ was shot horizontally from the crossbow with the string pulled back $50\,\text{cm}$. A speed meter showed the launch speed of the arrow to be $47.0\,\text{m/s}$.

a) Determine the spring constant from a line fitted to the measurement points and use it to calculate the energy stored in the crossbow in the pulled position.

b) Calculate the kinetic energy of the arrow at launch.

c) What percentage of the stored energy changed into the kinetic energy of the arrow? Where did the rest of the energy probably go?

Give the percentage of part c) in the answer box.
